headline: U.S. employers add more jobs than expected

sources.title: The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October and the unemployment rate fell (CNN Business)
U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October, way more than expected; unemployment rate slips to 4.1% (CNBC)
Hiring jumps: The economy added 165,000 jobs last month (NPR)

chunks.text: Hiring in the United States {{picked up}} [[sharply]] in October. On Friday, November 6, 2026, the Labor Department said [[employers]] added 165,000 jobs that month. The total {{came in}} far above [[forecasts]]. Economists had expected only about 60,000 new jobs. The [[unemployment rate]], the share of workers who want a job but do not have one, fell to 4.1 percent. In September, it was 4.2 percent.

verbs.wrong: To be counted twice by mistake
verbs.why: Business at the cafe picks up in the morning. Sales often pick up before the holidays. Hiring in the United States picked up sharply in October.

verbs.correct: To be reported as a certain number
verbs.wrong: To be guessed before it happens
verbs.why: Sales sometimes come in lower than the company hopes. The final bill usually comes in above the first price. The October jobs total came in far above forecasts.

chunks.text: The department also [[revised]], or updated, its numbers for August and September. Together, the updates {{add up to}} 84,000 more jobs than first reported. Hiring is much stronger than in 2025, when employers added only about 10,000 jobs a month. An economics professor at a university in Minnesota is [[cautious]]. He {{points out}} that hiring was also strong early in 2026. Then it {{slowed down}} over the summer. He wants to see if the [[gains]] {{hold up}}.

verbs.wrong: To be reported one month late
verbs.why: Small savings add up to a lot of money. Our monthly bills add up to about 2,000 dollars. The updates for August and September add up to 84,000 more jobs than first reported.

verbs.wrong: To count the number of jobs
verbs.why: My teacher points out my spelling mistakes. The doctor points out that sleep matters for health. An economics professor at a university in Minnesota points out that hiring was also strong early in 2026.

verbs.wrong: To pay workers less each hour
verbs.why: Sales slow down after the holidays. Business at the beach slows down in the fall. Hiring was strong early in 2026, but then it slowed down over the summer.

verbs.wrong: To be given to workers as pay
verbs.why: Strong sales rarely hold up for long. Low gas prices do not always hold up through the winter. The professor wants to see if the new job gains hold up.

chunks.text: The gains came from many kinds of work. Businesses that help other companies, such as accounting and [[law firms]], added the most jobs, with 70,000. Health care was next. [[Warehouses]] and transportation companies added about 25,000 jobs as stores {{gear up}} for the [[holiday shopping season]]. Not every [[industry]] grew. Restaurants and [[construction companies]] {{cut back}} on staff in October.

verbs.wrong: To close for a few days
verbs.why: Stores gear up for the holidays every fall. Schools gear up for the new year in August. Warehouses and transportation companies added jobs as stores gear up for the holiday shopping season.

verbs.correct: To reduce the number of something
verbs.wrong: To move workers to a new city
verbs.why: When sales are slow, many shops cut back on staff. Some hotels cut back on workers in the winter. Restaurants and construction companies cut back on staff in October.

chunks.text: Pay is the weaker part of the report. [[Average pay]] rose 3.1 percent from a year earlier. [[Energy prices]] rose in 2026. [[Overall]], prices in September were 3.7 percent higher than a year before. So pay is not {{keeping up with}} prices, and many workers are {{falling behind}}. Many investors expect the Federal Reserve, America's [[central bank]], to raise [[interest rates]] in December. That would {{push up}} the cost of [[borrowing]] money.

verbs.correct: To rise as fast as something else
verbs.wrong: To be paid on the same day
verbs.why: Her salary does not keep up with the cost of food. Pay often fails to keep up with rent in big cities. Average pay rose 3.1 percent, so it is not keeping up with prices.

verbs.correct: To not keep pace with rising prices
verbs.wrong: To lose a job to a computer
verbs.why: Workers fall behind when prices rise faster than pay. Families on small incomes often fall behind. With prices up 3.7 percent and pay up 3.1 percent, many workers are falling behind.

verbs.wrong: To make something easier to get
verbs.why: Bad weather often pushes up the price of fruit. Strong demand pushes up rents in big cities. A rate rise in December would push up the cost of borrowing money.

mainIdea.s: U.S. employers added far more jobs in October than economists had expected, and unemployment fell slightly. Still, pay is rising more slowly than prices, so many workers are falling behind.
mainIdea.why: Employers added 165,000 jobs when experts expected about 60,000. But pay rose 3.1 percent while prices rose 3.7 percent, so pay is not keeping up.

mainIdea.s: Hiring grew strongly across the country in October, led by restaurants and construction companies. Because wages now climb faster than the cost of living, most families can afford more than before.
mainIdea.why: Close, but restaurants and construction companies cut back on staff. Pay is also not keeping up with prices, so many workers are falling behind.

mainIdea.s: A government report says many American factories closed in October as orders from abroad dropped. Thousands of people lost their jobs, and joblessness climbed to its highest level in years.
mainIdea.why: The report showed strong hiring. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1 percent as hiring picked up.

tf.s: Hiring in the U.S. picked up sharply in October.
tf.why: Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than economists expected.

tf.s: The October jobs total came in below what economists expected.
tf.why: It came in far above forecasts. Economists expected only about 60,000 new jobs, but employers added 165,000.

tf.s: The unemployment rate rose in October.
tf.why: As hiring picked up, the unemployment rate fell to 4.1 percent from 4.2 percent.

tf.s: Every kind of business added workers in October.
tf.why: Not every industry grew. Restaurants and construction companies cut back on staff.

tf.s: Pay is not keeping up with rising prices.
tf.why: Average pay rose 3.1 percent, but prices were 3.7 percent higher in September, so many workers are falling behind.

tf.s: An economics professor is sure the strong hiring will last.
tf.why: He is cautious. He points out that hiring slowed down after a strong start to 2026, so he wants to see if the gains hold up.

lines.text: Did you see the October jobs report?
The opposite. Hiring {{picked up}} a lot. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October.
Only about 60,000. So the total {{came in}} way above that.
Maybe not. The numbers for August and September went higher too. The changes {{add up to}} 84,000 more jobs.
So it's more than one good month. Which jobs grew?
Business services added the most. Warehouses hired too, since stores {{gear up}} for the holidays.
Yes. Restaurants and construction companies {{cut back}} on staff.
What about pay? Prices are [[on the rise]] everywhere.
That's [[the flip side]]. Pay rose 3.1 percent, but prices were 3.7 percent higher in September.
So pay isn't {{keeping up with}} prices.
Right. A lot of workers are {{falling behind}}. The good news comes with [[a reality check]].
And if the Fed raises rates in December, that will {{push up}} the cost of loans.
True. One economics professor also says hiring {{slowed down}} over the summer, so he wants to see if the gains {{hold up}}.
I hope they do. People need some [[breathing room]].

expressions.def: Used to talk about the other, less pleasant part of a situation

expressions.def: Something that makes you see the true situation, which is often less good
ex: My first electric bill was a reality check.
The test was a reality check for the whole class.

expressions.def: Extra time, money or space that makes a situation less stressful
ex: A small raise would give us some breathing room.
